identification.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks Storm-3075 as an initial access broker and malware distributor that it assesses delivers final payloads on behalf of multiple downstream actors [S1]. Microsoft describes it as using AI-themed malvertising to distribute payloads [S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft's first public description found is the 2026-06-08 blog; it states malvertising activity since at least early 2026, with a documented campaign run on 2026-03-13 [S1]. Microsoft lists no aliases [S1]. Storm-3075 is a Microsoft developing-cluster designation. The malware-signing service used in the documented campaign is attributed by Microsoft to a separate actor, Fox Tempest; the two clusters should not be merged [S1][S3].

attribution.basis: Microsoft characterizes the actor as an initial access broker and malware distributor and describes related actors (Fox Tempest) as financially motivated [S1]. No state sponsor, nationality, or government attribution was found in the sources reviewed.

objectives: Microsoft assesses Storm-3075 acts as an initial access broker and malware distributor delivering final payloads for multiple downstream actors, with payloads including information stealers and loaders [S1]. A specific monetization model is not stated in the sources reviewed.

targeting.notes: Microsoft reports the 2026-03-13 campaign run targeted over 66,000 devices, with Japan, South Africa, the United States and France the top affected countries, and assesses most impacted devices were likely consumer endpoints [S1]. Victims were likely first exposed through free movie streaming sites [S1]. No sector targeting was identified.

capabilities.summary: Documented delivery chain (March 2026): malvertising on free movie streaming sites redirected victims to a page advertising a fictitious 'Awesome AI Windows plugin'; the download, ProFluxeFlowAi-win-Setup.exe, was hosted in a GitHub repository and required manual launch [S1]. The installer showed a 'Continue' checkbox that blocked execution until clicked, which Microsoft assesses was intended to evade sandboxes [S1]. It then dropped a Python interpreter (pythonw.exe) and a downloader script (LICENSE.txt) in an AppData\Local folder, and the script ran shellcode that fetched the next stage from the C2 domain brokeapt[.]com [S1]. The payload in the documented campaign was Vidar stealer; Microsoft also observed the campaign distributing Lumma Stealer, Hijack Loader and Oyster [S1]. The executable was signed with a fraudulently obtained Microsoft-issued certificate, which Microsoft attributes to the Fox Tempest malware-signing-as-a-service offering [S1]. Microsoft revoked the certificate and GitHub removed the repository, which Microsoft says helped prevent tens of thousands of additional infections [S1].

campaigns.name: brokeapt[.]com loader infrastructure
campaigns.summary: Microsoft lists brokeapt[.]com, the C2 for the Python loader, as seen from 2026-03-10 to 2026-05-20 [S1].

campaigns.name: Fake 'Awesome AI Windows plugin' malvertising run
campaigns.summary: A single campaign run targeted over 66,000 devices via streaming-site malvertising and a GitHub-hosted fake AI plugin installer that delivered Vidar; Vidar C2 domains pan.ssffaa19[.]xyz and pan.rongtv[.]xyz were seen 2026-03-13 to 2026-03-14 [S1]. Microsoft revoked the signing certificate and GitHub removed the repository [S1].

campaigns.name: Fox Tempest signing-service disruption (context)
campaigns.summary: Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit disrupted Fox Tempest's malware-signing-as-a-service operation, which abused Microsoft Artifact Signing to generate short-lived fraudulent code-signing certificates [S3]. Microsoft says it has revoked over one thousand certificates attributed to Fox Tempest [S1]. This is a related but separate cluster.

campaigns.name: Microsoft public reporting on AI-branded lures
campaigns.summary: Microsoft published 'AI brands as bait', naming Storm-3075 and detailing the March campaign [S1]. A 2026-09-10 Microsoft post again cites Storm-3075 as an initial access broker using AI-themed malvertising to distribute payloads [S2].

diamond.adversary: Storm-3075, a Microsoft-tracked initial access broker and malware distributor serving multiple downstream actors [S1]. Individual operators and downstream customers are not identified in the sources reviewed.
diamond.capability: AI-themed malvertising, GitHub-hosted fake installer, sandbox-evasion user-interaction gate, Python-based downloader with shellcode, Vidar/Lumma/Hijack Loader/Oyster payloads, fraudulently signed binaries [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Free streaming-site ad redirects, a GitHub repository ('shippingtechnologymovie', folder 'AI-techVideos', since removed), loader C2 brokeapt[.]com, Vidar C2 pan.ssffaa19[.]xyz and pan.rongtv[.]xyz, and a fraudulent Microsoft-issued code-signing certificate (SHA-1 thumbprint 4f5c5b3ef45cfff7721754487a86aeff9a2e6e32) [S1].
diamond.victim: Primarily consumer endpoints, with the top affected countries Japan, South Africa, the United States and France [S1].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints, web browsers and ad networks on streaming sites, GitHub hosting, and Microsoft code-signing trust (certificate-based reputation) [S1][S3].

gaps: Microsoft's blog is the only primary source found; independent vendor confirmation of the 66,000-device figure and the Storm-3075 attribution was not located.
Downstream actors receiving Storm-3075 access are not named in sources reviewed [S1].
Operator identity, origin, and sponsor are unknown; no government attribution found.
Whether Storm-3075 overlaps with other vendor clusters (a third-party blog title pairs 'Storm-3075 & o1oo1' but could not be opened) is unverified.
Sector targeting and targeting of enterprise or government networks are not documented.
The Microsoft 2026-09-10 post does not itself link Storm-3075 to the fake plugin campaign [S2].
Several secondary articles (securityarsenal.com, securityweek.com, boerse-express.com) could not be fetched; claims from them are not used.
No MITRE ATT&CK group identifier exists in the actor record.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2 (environment/effects): the actor's reach is consumer endpoints via streaming-site malvertising, so direct effect on DoD networks is indirect, mainly through personal devices, credential theft from stealers, and downstream access resale [S1]. Step 3 (adversary): a commodity access broker with multiple customers; intent of downstream buyers is unknown [S1]. Step 4 MLCOA: continued AI-branded lure campaigns delivering infostealers and loaders to consumer devices, with stolen credentials feeding later intrusions [S1][S2]. MDCOA (analyst inference, not sourced): the resold access reaches personnel or contractor devices and is used by a more capable downstream actor. Candidate indicators: brokeapt[.]com, pan.ssffaa19[.]xyz, pan.rongtv[.]xyz, installer ProFluxeFlowAi-win-Setup.exe (SHA-256 c7c5072df9f83f4c440a5c3bb4be1d5f6c67bbf78f196406ca20d27b43b975b8), pythonw.exe plus LICENSE.txt in AppData\Local, and the fraudulent signer thumbprint above [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track Microsoft reporting on Storm-3075 and add the published domains, hash and certificate thumbprint to detection watchlists [S1]. Authorities: blocking and network-monitoring actions on mission networks remain under the owning network operator's authorities; coordination with personnel on personal-device use is a policy matter. Mission assurance: infostealer exposure of credentials and session tokens argues for phishing-resistant MFA and rapid credential reset on suspected exposure, consistent with Microsoft's mitigation guidance (phishing-resistant MFA, SmartScreen, network protection, Defender attack disruption) [S1]. Coordination: report suspected infections through the appropriate cyber defense and reporting channels and share indicators with partners; code-signing alone should not be treated as proof of legitimacy given the fraudulent certificate abuse [S1][S3].
